A published prompt or workflow specification, openly licensed, restructured into these fields. Nobody has reported running it and writing up what happened. It is a design someone published, not a design with a history — the difference is recorded on every one of these records.

aside.label: The instructor’s own work
aside.reads: Not governed by a course AI policy. Institutional policy on staff use, and any disclosure your discipline expects of authors, still apply.

policy.note: Every activity in the collection carries the position it assumes. That is derived from the record — from whether the model touches submitted work, whether the work is assessed, and what disclosure the design asks for — not from anyone’s view about what a course policy ought to say. An activity sitting at one position is not a recommendation to adopt that position.

source.name: Classroom Policies for AI Generative Tools
source.note: The worked examples below were drawn from this open, crowdsourced collection of course AI policies, which is added to continuously. Each quotation keeps the instructor, the course, the institution and the license the contributor placed it under. The four positions are a reading of that collection, not a scheme anyone has to adopt.

tiers.gist: AI is welcome for studying and skill-building, but never for the work you submit.

items.quote: You are expected to use the university's AI tutor each week as a study coach … [but] do not use any AI to generate answers for homework, worksheets, or projects. Copying or paraphrasing AI output is prohibited.

Don't. Unless you receive explicit instructor permission, do not submit materials produced by … 'generative AI' in this course. You also may not use them for research or summarization of course materials.

No AI use for writing assignments … is permitted … Using tools for spellcheck and grammar is perfectly fine — and recommended. [This] class is carefully designed to help you learn the subject, think critically, and write thoughtfully.
All assignments should be prepared by the student… AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism.
Please do not use Generative AI tools as a substitute for your own thinking, reflections, and voice… None of you are mediocre, and you deserve better.

tiers.label: Practice, not products
tiers.reads: Runs in a course where nothing the model touched may be handed in.
tiers.rule: the model is held back from the submitted work, or nothing graded comes out of it

tiers.gist: Generative AI is off-limits unless an instructor explicitly allows it — often case by case.

items.quote: Students … are not permitted to utilize Generative AI at any stage … unless explicitly noted in the instructions for a deliverable. Students may formally request, in writing, an exception … considered on a case-by-case basis.

Students are allowed to employ generative A.I. tools in specific exercises when instructed so … If an A.I. tool is actually used, an addendum must be turned in with each exercise, with a live link to the chat for accountability.

items.course: Sample statement: “use only with prior permission”
items.quote: Students are allowed to use … (artificial intelligence … such as ChatGPT or Dall-E) on assignments … if instructor permission is obtained in advance. Unless given permission …, each student is expected to complete each assignment without … automated tools.
Use of generative AI tools only with prior permission… you must highlight information retrieved using generative AI and cite it properly.
In general, you may not use AI to complete homework or group work assignments. If you are permitted to use it for a specific assignment, I will say so.

tiers.label: By permission only
tiers.reads: Needs the instructor to have said, for this assignment, that the tool is allowed.
tiers.rule: the model enters assessed work under the instructor’s own authorisation

tiers.gist: Use is optional — but if you use it, trace it, cite it, and own the output.

items.quote: You will never be required to use AI … Work created with generative AI will likely lead to a lower grade … If you use AI, you must trace its claims to sources, cite them, and remain accountable for the information.

AI is a tool, not a shortcut! … You are accountable for all work with your name on it … For every assignment, students shall include an AI disclosure statement specifying which tools were used, how they contributed, and the portions they influenced.

The key goal of our course … is to use words, sources, and technology tools in transparent, accountable, and ethical ways … If you decide to use a Generative AI tool … reflect that use in your submitted work.
The burden does not fall on the instructor to prove that AI was used, but rather on the student to prove that learning has occurred.
When using AI to research topics, you must cite any information obtained from AI sources, just as you would with books, articles, or websites.
AI is a tool, but one that you need to acknowledge using… Using these tools without proper citation constitutes plagiarism.

tiers.label: Disclose & be accountable
tiers.reads: Comes with its own disclosure: the design already asks for a log, a trace or a statement.
tiers.rule: the activity itself requires the use to be recorded

tiers.gist: AI use is encouraged when it supports learning — just cite how you used it.

items.quote: You are welcome to use AI tools … unless otherwise specified. However, you must cite it as a source, including a description of how you used it … Thoughtful use is encouraged; use that replaces learning is frowned upon.

I encourage you to use AI-related technologies in this class … For research, AI use is encouraged … For coding, you are welcome to treat AI as a tutor … For written content, please write a draft … before using AI to help improve it.

This course encourages the … ethical/responsible use of AI/ML, Generative AI, and Agentic tools … What I ask in return is (1) transparency in use, and (2) willingness to share … prompts, code, and other artifacts.
AI writing tools can be helpful resources for thinking as well as writing. I encourage students to use them to think through questions throughout the course.
You are encouraged to explore the use of generative AI tools to improve learning… you are responsible for ensuring the accuracy, ethics, and proper citation of any information generated.

tiers.label: Welcomed, with citation
tiers.reads: Assumes use is fine and asks the student to say how the tool was used.
tiers.rule: the activity asks only for an acknowledgement

general: Consider what information you and your students will put into a tool, and where it goes.
Consider whether every participant can access the tool at no cost, without creating a personal account, and with assistive technology.
Consider how outputs will be checked, and who remains responsible for the final work.
Consider how use of the tool will be acknowledged, in line with your course policy and your discipline's expectations.
intro: The activities in this collection do not name a product as a requirement. Each one records what a tool has to be able to do: hold a text conversation, answer over a document you supply, make an image, and so on. This page describes those kinds of systems in general terms, so you can recognize which kind a tool belongs to — whatever it is called this year.

Many current products combine several of these capabilities, and features appear, change and disappear frequently. Before you build a course activity around any tool, consider checking what your institution provides, what the tool does with the information you give it, and whether every participant can access it.

no_ai.name: Activities that use no AI tool
no_ai.text: Some activities are designed so that no AI tool is used at all — for example, examining AI-generated examples supplied in advance, or discussing AI without using it. Others describe a route that works without AI. What If AI lets you ask for these directly.

types.does: Drafts, summarizes, rephrases, explains, brainstorms, answers questions and responds to feedback in plain language.
types.io: In: typed instructions, questions or pasted text. Out: text — prose, lists, outlines, tables or code.
types.limits: Output can be fluent and wrong, including invented references and quotations. Responses vary from one attempt to the next, reflect patterns in training data (including biases), and may not reflect recent events unless the system is connected to search. Anything you paste in may be retained, depending on the service and your institution's agreement with it.
types.name: General-purpose conversational AI
types.what: A large language model you interact with through conversation. It predicts and generates text in response to what you write, and can keep track of the earlier turns in the same conversation.
types.why: This is the kind of tool most people mean by 'AI' in teaching. Most activities in the collection need at least this capability, whether the model is used as a drafting partner, a conversation partner, or the object being examined.

types.does: Finds and summarizes relevant passages, answers questions about the material, compares documents and points back to the sections it drew on.
types.io: In: uploaded files or linked sources, plus questions. Out: answers, summaries or notes, usually with references to passages in the supplied material.
types.limits: Answers are only as good as what is retrieved; the system can still misread, over-generalize or miss passages. Pointers to sources need checking. Uploading documents raises copyright, privacy and data-retention questions, especially for student work or unpublished material.
types.name: Document-grounded assistants
types.what: A system that answers from a set of documents you supply — readings, a syllabus, transcripts, a dataset description — rather than only from what the model learned in training. This is often called retrieval-augmented generation.
types.why: Useful when an activity should stay inside a defined set of sources, such as course readings, or when a task involves working across a large body of your own material.

types.does: Searches, gathers and summarizes sources, suggests related literature and attaches links or citations to its answers.
types.io: In: a question or search terms. Out: a synthesized answer with links, citations or lists of papers.
types.limits: Coverage depends on what the system can reach; paywalled and specialist sources are often missing. Citations can be mismatched to claims, and summaries can overstate what a source says. Consider checking key claims against the original source and against library databases.
types.name: Search- and research-oriented AI
types.what: A system that retrieves current or external information — from the web, a scholarly index or a database — and composes a response from what it finds.
types.why: Faculty encounter these in literature searching, fact-checking and research workflows, and students increasingly use them in place of conventional search.

types.does: Describes and interprets images, extracts text from scans, explains figures and answers questions about what an image shows.
types.io: In: images or files plus a question. Out: text descriptions, transcriptions or explanations.
types.limits: Interpretations can be confidently wrong, especially for specialist images, small details, handwriting and charts. Images may contain identifiable people or sensitive information; consider whether they should be uploaded at all.
types.name: Multimodal AI that reads images and documents
types.what: A model that accepts images — photographs, scanned pages, charts, diagrams, screenshots — as input alongside text.
types.why: Relevant to activities involving visual sources, lab or field images, handwritten material, data visualizations and accessibility tasks such as drafting image descriptions.

types.does: Creates illustrations, concept images, visual variations and mock-ups.
types.io: In: a text prompt, sometimes with a reference image. Out: one or more images.
types.limits: Outputs can reproduce stereotypes and defaults, and can closely resemble existing works. Questions about copyright, attribution and the use of artists' work in training remain unsettled. Generated images of real people or events can mislead if they are not labeled.
types.name: Image generation
types.what: A system that produces new images from a text description, and in some cases edits or extends an existing image.
types.why: Appears in studio, design and media courses, in materials preparation, and in activities that examine how generated images represent people, places and ideas.

types.does: Generates or animates scenes, creates explainer-style clips and produces talking-head video from a script.
types.io: In: a text prompt, a script, images or video. Out: video clips.
types.limits: Access is often limited or paid, and outputs are short and uneven in quality. Synthetic video of realistic people raises consent, disclosure and misinformation concerns; consider how any generated video will be labeled.
types.name: Video generation
types.what: A system that produces short video clips from text, images or existing footage, sometimes including synthetic presenters.
types.why: Encountered in media production, course materials and discussions of synthetic media and misinformation.

types.does: Transcribes lectures, interviews and meetings; reads text aloud; produces narration in a synthetic voice; composes short pieces of music or sound.
types.io: In: recordings, text or a prompt. Out: transcripts, spoken audio or generated audio.
types.limits: Transcription accuracy drops with accents, specialist vocabulary, crosstalk and poor recordings, so transcripts need checking. Recordings of people are personal data and may require consent or ethics approval. Cloned or synthetic voices raise consent and impersonation concerns.
types.name: Speech, audio and voice
types.what: Systems that work with sound: speech recognition (transcription), text-to-speech and synthetic voice, and generation of music or other audio.
types.why: Common in accessibility work (captions, audio versions of text), qualitative research (interview transcription), language learning and media projects.

types.does: Suggests and debugs code, explains programs, runs analyses, produces charts and summarizes results.
types.io: In: code, data files or a description of an analysis. Out: code, charts, tables and written interpretations.
types.limits: Code can run and still be wrong; analyses can apply inappropriate methods or silently mishandle data. Consider reviewing the code, not only the result. Uploading research or student data raises confidentiality and data-management questions.
types.name: Coding assistants and data analysis
types.what: Systems that write, explain and run code, including tools that analyze an uploaded dataset by writing and executing code on your behalf.
types.why: Relevant to programming courses, quantitative methods, research data work and any activity where students or faculty analyze data.

types.does: Chains steps together: gathering information, filling in documents, sorting records, drafting and sending messages or updating systems.
types.io: In: a goal or instruction and access to other tools or data. Out: completed tasks, documents or changes in connected systems.
types.limits: Errors can compound across steps and be harder to notice. Consider what the system is allowed to access or change, where a person reviews its work, and who is accountable for the result.
types.name: Agentic and workflow-automation systems
types.what: Systems in which a model carries out multi-step tasks — calling other tools, moving between applications or taking actions — with some degree of autonomy.
types.why: Appears mainly in administrative and research workflows, such as screening literature or processing routine documents.

types.does: Offers similar capabilities under negotiated terms — for example, limits on how submitted data is retained or used, sign-in with institutional credentials, and access for everyone in a course.
types.limits: Institutional terms differ, and not every feature is available in every environment. Consider checking your institution's guidance on approved tools and data classification before using any AI tool with student work, research data or confidential information.
types.name: Institutionally hosted and private AI environments
types.what: Versions of the systems above provided through an institutional agreement, or run on infrastructure the institution controls, rather than accessed through a personal account.
types.why: Several activities ask what goes into a model and who can access the tool. An institutionally provided option can change the answer to both, and can remove the need for students to create personal accounts or pay.

types.does: Performs a specialized analysis or prediction, often inside research software or a programming environment.
types.io: In: domain data such as images, sequences, measurements or text corpora. Out: classifications, predictions, measurements or structured results.
types.limits: Results depend heavily on the data a model was trained on and may not transfer to local conditions. Validation against known cases and disciplinary judgment remain essential.
types.name: Discipline-specific AI and machine learning
types.what: Models built for a particular field or task — for example, analyzing microscope images, predicting molecular structures, classifying specimens or modeling domain data. Many are not generative chat systems at all.
types.why: Faculty in the sciences, health professions and data-intensive fields encounter these in research and in methods courses. Some activities in this collection teach how such models work and how to check their outputs.
